### 1.2 A-Tier venues

**PVLDB Volume 20 / VLDB 2027** — databases. `verified`
- Deadline: rolling, 1st of each month, 17:00 Pacific, with **mandatory abstract by the 25th of the
  previous month**. Next usable: abstract 2026-09-25, paper 2026-10-01. Final cycle deadline 2027-03-01.
- Notification: initial reviews on the 15th of the following month. One revision permitted, up to 2.5 months.
- Page limit: 12 pages excluding references for Regular Research and for **Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark
  (EA&B)**; 6 pages for Vision. Appendices count inside the limit.
- Anonymous review: **no** — VLDB is single-blind, names required on page 1.
- Artifact: supplemental material is **mandatory** (or an explicit justification for withholding it);
  ACM "Artifacts Available" badge for accepted papers that comply; optional PVLDB Reproducibility
  Evaluation. EA&B papers must release everything, no excuses, **with the reproducibility package linked
  in the initial submission**.
- Source: https://www.vldb.org/2027/submission-guidelines.html
- Fit: the EA&B category is the closest formal match in any venue to what this project actually is — "the
  scientific contribution lies in providing new insights into the strengths and weaknesses of existing
  methods rather than in providing new methods." Against that: the PVLDB Scope Policy requires (i) a core
  data-management contribution, (ii) non-superficial engagement with the DB literature, and (iii)
  evaluation grounded in data-management applications. A paper whose headline metric is LLM-graded answer
  correctness will be scope-tested hard. The federation-vs-merging result (1,083 of 9,138 nodes edited;
  a third graph loadable only under federation) is the part that is legible as data management; the
  correctness table is not.

### 1.5 Journals

**Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR).** `verified`
- Rolling submission, no deadline. Submissions paused annually over the December holidays (in 2025 that
  was 2025-12-02 to 2026-01-05); assume a similar pause around December 2026.
- Page limit: **none** — "variable manuscript length" is an explicit design feature.
- Anonymous review: **yes**, double-blind, hosted publicly on OpenReview.
- Acceptance criteria, verbatim in substance: (1) are the claims supported by accurate, convincing and
  clear evidence, and (2) would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings. TMLR
  "emphasizes technical correctness over subjective significance." Where claims outrun evidence, authors
  are asked to *narrow the claims*.
- Source: https://jmlr.org/tmlr/ and https://jmlr.org/tmlr/acceptance-criteria.html
- Fit: TMLR's criterion is the single most favourable in this report for a project with strong internal
  evidence and no external baseline — because "no external baseline" is a *scope-of-claim* problem at TMLR,
  not a *rejection* trigger. The risk is audience: TMLR is a machine-learning journal and no model is
  trained here. An action editor could reasonably desk it as out of audience.

**Semantic Web Journal (IOS Press).** `verified`
- Permanent open calls, **no fixed deadline**. Paper types include Full research papers, Survey articles,
  Application reports, and **Reports on tools and systems**.
- Page limit: none imposed by the call.
- Review: **open and transparent** — reviews and reviewer names are published alongside the paper.
  Not anonymous, in either direction, by design.
- Artifact: no formal badging; the community norm is a resolvable, persistent artifact.
- Source: https://www.semantic-web-journal.net/calls
- Both currently-listed special issues (LLMs/GenAI+KGs, 2025-03-31; Cultural Heritage, 2025-04-30) are
  **expired**. The permanent calls are the live route.
- Fit: best overall fit in this report. Exact domain (federated KGs, query languages, KG QA), no page limit
  for a four-finding paper with a 41-experiment appendix, no deadline pressure, and a community whose
  flagship conference states in writing that negative results should be reported.

**Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research (JAIR).** `verified`
- Rolling, no deadline. Decision in ~8–12 weeks. **At most one resubmission.** No fees.
- Page limit: none, but "we strongly encourage authors to be concise."
- Anonymous review: single-blind (reviewers anonymous to authors; authors are not anonymised).
- **A completed reproducibility checklist is mandatory — submissions without it are desk-rejected.**
- Submission requires three free-text answers, one of which is: name 1–3 prior JAIR papers closest to
  your work and say how yours differs. "Articles with little similarity in content or structure to
  published JAIR articles have a high chance of rejection without review."
- Explicit summary-rejection categories include: "Papers merely apply known AI techniques to a problem or
  problem area, but do not provide insights or methodological contributions of significant interest to the
  AI research community," and "Papers that are insufficiently grounded in the state of the art."
- Source: https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/about/submissions
- Fit: risky. The first summary-rejection category above is close to how a hostile reader would describe an
  applied KGQA system, and JAIR is the strictest venue here on demanding a *general AI* insight. The
  grader-calibration result is the only part of this project that clears that bar unaided.

## 2. Tier definitions and requirement checklists

This is the deliverable. Each item is written so that a person holding the project's evidence list can
answer **yes / no / partially** without further judgement calls.

### 2.1 A-Tier

**Definition.** A top-tier archival venue: proceedings indexed and permanent; a multi-layer program
committee (reviewers, then area chairs, then senior area chairs or PC chairs) with a rebuttal or author-
response stage; a published desk-reject policy enforced mechanically; and the field's own top ranking
signal.

**Signal used.** CORE A* where CORE ranks the venue, plus CSRankings-counted status for the
databases/IR/NLP subfields. *I could not load portal.core.edu.au (JavaScript shell), so the specific CORE
grades below are `inferred` from general knowledge, not verified: VLDB A*, WWW A*, SIGIR A*, NAACL A,
ISWC A.* Where the ranking is inferred I have leaned on the structural signals I could verify instead —
mandatory abstract pre-registration, submission caps, scope policies, mechanical desk rejection — all of
which VLDB, WWW and ARR publish and all of which are A-Tier behaviour.

| id | heading | requirement | blocking |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | novelty | Is the central claim new to the *published literature* (not merely new to this system), with at least one cited prior publication that makes the closest competing claim and an explicit statement of the difference? | yes |
| A2 | novelty | Can the headline contribution be restated as a finding that transfers to systems the authors did not build, rather than as a description of one system's behaviour? | yes |
| A3 | novelty | If a headline result is null or negative, does the paper cite at least two published works asserting the belief it contradicts, so that the null has a target? | no |
| A4 | evidence | Is at least one reported comparison run on a question set, benchmark, or corpus that the authors did not author? | yes |
| A5 | evidence | Does every number in the headline table come from at least three independent runs, with the random seeds recorded and variance or standard deviation reported? | yes |
| A6 | evidence | Are the main results reproduced in at least two distinct domains, or on at least two schema/query-language pairs beyond the original one? | no |
| A7 | evidence | Is every pairwise difference reported with a confidence interval or a named statistical test, and is every interval that crosses zero described in the text as not established? | yes |
| A8 | evidence | Is there either a human evaluation, or a validation of the automatic grader against human labels on a stated sample with a reported agreement statistic (e.g. Cohen's kappa, Kendall tau)? | yes |
| A9 | evidence | Was the held-out test set used exactly once, is its size stated, and is there an explicit statement that no tuning decision was informed by it? | no |
| A10 | baselines | Is at least one baseline a **published external system**, either re-run by the authors or quoted from its own paper on the identical data and metric? Internal ablations do not satisfy this item. | yes |
| A11 | baselines | Does the related-work section name the three closest published systems and, for each, either include it in the evaluation or give a specific stated reason it could not be run? | yes |
| A12 | writing | Does the submission fit the venue's page limit counting appendices where that venue counts them (VLDB 12 excl. refs; WWW 8 content / 12 total; ARR long 8; ECIR 12 incl. appendices)? | yes |
| A13 | writing | Is there an explicit limitations section that names every known threat to validity, including each deliberately-unfixed scoring fault, and states the *direction* and an *upper bound* on the bias each introduces? | yes |
| A14 | artifact | Are code, data pointers, and run configurations deposited in an archival repository with a resolvable **DOI** at submission time, anonymised where the venue is double-blind? | no |
| A15 | disqualifier | Would the submission survive mechanical desk-reject checks at the target venue: anonymity, formatting, page limit, pre-registered abstract by the stated date, declared conflicts of interest, and the venue's written scope policy? | yes |

### 2.2 B-Tier

**Definition.** A solid archival venue with permanent indexed proceedings and a real program committee,
selective but below the field's top band — CORE A or B, or a top-band conference's secondary track (short
papers, in-use, resources). Acceptance rates typically 20–30%. Reviewing is usually two to three reviewers
plus a meta-reviewer, often with a rebuttal, but without the multi-layer SAC escalation of A-Tier.

**Signal used.** CORE A/B (`inferred`: EDBT A, ECIR B/A, CIKM B/A, ESWC A/B), plus the structural test that
the venue publishes proceedings in a permanent series (Springer LNCS for ECIR and ESWC; the EDBT
proceedings series) and runs a rebuttal or revision stage.

| id | heading | requirement | blocking |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | novelty | Is there a stated contribution that a reader could act on without adopting the authors' codebase — a finding, a method, or a measured trade-off? | yes |
| B2 | novelty | Is a measurement-only contribution acceptable here? At ESWC and ECIR: yes, provided the measurement isolates a named variable. Does this paper name the single variable each comparison isolates? | yes |
| B3 | novelty | Are negative results explicitly framed as the contribution rather than buried, and does the paper say what a practitioner should now do differently? | no |
| B4 | evidence | Does every headline number come from at least two independent runs, with any single-run number labelled in the table as `n=1`? | yes |
| B5 | evidence | Is the primary test set at least ~200 items per arm, and is its provenance (who wrote the questions, how they were split) stated in the paper body rather than an appendix? | yes |
| B6 | evidence | Are confidence intervals reported for every difference the paper claims, and is every interval that includes zero described in prose as unestablished rather than as a positive result? | yes |
| B7 | evidence | Where correctness is machine-graded, are at least two independent grader families used, and is disagreement between them reported rather than averaged away? | yes |
| B8 | evidence | Is there at least one *countable, non-graded* measure supporting a headline claim (a count of records, edits, nodes, or provable declines) that does not depend on any language model's judgement? | no |
| B9 | baselines | Internal ablations may serve as the primary comparison, but is there at least one **external anchor** — a published system, a published number on a comparable task, or a documented off-the-shelf tool — positioning the absolute scores? | yes |
| B10 | baselines | Does the paper state explicitly and in the body, not a footnote, that no external system was run, and why? | yes |
| B11 | writing | Does the related-work section cover every community the work touches (KG question answering, federated/virtual integration, text-to-query generation, LLM-as-judge evaluation) with recent citations from the target venue's own proceedings? | no |
| B12 | writing | Is there a limitations section, and does it disclose each deliberately-unfixed scoring fault with its direction of bias? | yes |
| B13 | artifact | Is there a supplemental-material statement pointing to code and data with a persistent identifier (ESWC requires this and reviewers score it), anonymised for review? | yes |
| B14 | disqualifier | Is the submission properly anonymised (ESWC rejects on anonymisation failure alone; ECIR desk-rejects on page overrun) and within the page limit counting appendices? | yes |
| B15 | disqualifier | Does any headline sentence in the abstract or introduction assert a result whose confidence interval crosses zero? If yes, that is a rejection-grade overclaim at this tier. | yes |

### 2.3 Workshop / short paper

**Definition.** Either non-archival (no formal proceedings) or lightly archival (CEUR, or the ACL
Anthology). Two to three reviewers, no rebuttal, acceptance typically 40–60%. The purpose is community
feedback and priority-staking, not permanent record. **Note:** an ACL Anthology workshop *is* archival for
dual-submission purposes — publishing there consumes the work's unpublished status at most conferences.

**Signal used.** Presence of a workshop proceedings series, page limits of 4–8 pages, and a call that
solicits work in progress, position papers, or negative results.

| id | heading | requirement | blocking |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | novelty | Is there one crisp claim a reader could disagree with, stated in the abstract? | yes |
| W2 | novelty | Preliminary, partial, and negative results are in scope. Is the work's incompleteness stated up front rather than concealed? | yes |
| W3 | evidence | Is there at least one quantitative result with a stated sample size? | yes |
| W4 | evidence | Is `n_runs` stated for every reported number, even where it is 1? | yes |
| W5 | evidence | Does the paper state which numbers were produced by a language model grading a language model, so a reader is not misled about the instrument? | yes |
| W6 | baselines | Internal ablations are sufficient. Is the ablated variable named exactly, and is it the *only* thing that differs between the compared arms? | yes |
| W7 | baselines | Is the absence of an external system baseline stated in one sentence in the paper? | no |
| W8 | writing | Does the paper fit the workshop limit (NORA: 8 pages research / 6 position / 2 short, references and appendices excluded)? | yes |
| W9 | writing | Is a Limitations section present where the workshop mandates it (ACL-family workshops do), and a Declaration on Generative AI where required? | yes |
| W10 | writing | Is the paper's topical fit to *this specific workshop's* theme stated in the first page, rather than assumed? | yes |
| W11 | artifact | Is a code or data link present, anonymised if the review is double-blind? A DOI is not required at this tier. | no |
| W12 | disqualifier | Is the work free of a concurrent submission elsewhere? NORA desk-rejects undisclosed concurrent submissions to *archival or non-archival* venues alike. | yes |
| W13 | disqualifier | If the workshop is archival (ACL Anthology, CEUR with proceedings), is the team willing to spend the work's unpublished status here rather than saving it for a conference or journal? | yes |

### 2.4 Journal

**Definition.** No page limit, iterative revision over months, and — at TMLR and SWJ specifically — an
acceptance criterion built on *correctness and completeness* rather than on novelty or significance.
Journals are the only tier at this list's disposal where "we could not run an external system" is a
disclosure rather than a rejection.

**Signal used.** Published acceptance criteria (TMLR's are explicit and public), open or transparent review
(SWJ publishes reviews and reviewer names), and no length constraint.

| id | heading | requirement | blocking |
|---|---|---|---|
| J1 | novelty | Is the claim original and unpublished, with any overlap with prior workshop or conference papers by the same authors declared at submission? | yes |
| J2 | novelty | Novelty of *method* is not required (TMLR: technical correctness over subjective significance; SWJ accepts tool and system reports). Is there at least one reader in the journal's stated audience who would act on this finding, and can the paper name who? | yes |
| J3 | novelty | Are negative and null results acceptable? Yes at TMLR and SWJ. Is each null result stated as a null — "we could not detect a difference of size X" — rather than as an absence of effect? | yes |
| J4 | evidence | Is every claim in the abstract traceable to a specific experiment identifier reported in the paper or its appendix? | yes |
| J5 | evidence | Where the evidence does not support the broadest reading of a claim, has the *claim* been narrowed to match — this is TMLR's explicit remedy — rather than the evidence overstated? | yes |
| J6 | evidence | Is `n_runs`, seed status, and grader identity disclosed per experiment, including for the older experiments where `n_runs: 1` and seeds are unrecorded? | yes |
| J7 | evidence | Is the grader itself characterised — its failure modes, the smallest quality difference it can resolve, and which of the paper's results fall inside that resolution limit? | yes |
| J8 | evidence | Is there a stated scope boundary: exactly one domain, two schemas, two query languages, and no claim generalised past it? | yes |
| J9 | baselines | External published baselines are **not** mandatory at TMLR or SWJ. Is their absence stated, with the claims narrowed accordingly (e.g. "relative to the arms compared here" rather than "state of the art")? | yes |
| J10 | baselines | Is the related work complete enough that a reader can locate the external systems themselves, even though none were run? | yes |
| J11 | writing | Is there no page limit being exploited as an excuse for length — i.e. is the paper as long as its evidence requires and no longer (JAIR: "we strongly encourage authors to be concise")? | no |
| J12 | writing | Are the superseded experiments in the record described — that six experiments exist only because earlier measurements were wrong, and the wrong versions are retained and marked — since this is a credibility asset at journal review and invisible everywhere else? | no |
| J13 | artifact | Are code, data pointers and the experimental record released under a persistent identifier (DOI), with the license and attribution stated? SWJ and JWS reviewers expect resolvable, permanent resources. | yes |
| J14 | artifact | Where the journal mandates a reproducibility checklist (JAIR desk-rejects without one), is it completed and attached? | yes |
| J15 | disqualifier | Is the paper free of the "merely applies known techniques to an application area without a methodological contribution of general interest" reading, which JAIR lists as a summary-rejection category? | yes |

## 3. Calling the shot

### 3.1 The single venue I would submit to

**Semantic Web Journal (IOS Press), full research paper, permanent open call.**
https://www.semantic-web-journal.net/calls

Reasons, in order of weight:

1. **It is the only venue whose stated standards this project already meets without new experiments.**
   No page limit, so all four findings plus the grader-calibration study plus the 41-experiment record can
   be reported in one document instead of being amputated to fit 8 or 12 pages. No external-baseline
   mandate. Rolling submission, so no deadline forces a rushed write-up.
2. **Domain fit is exact.** Federated and decentralised knowledge graphs, query processing over knowledge
   graphs, and LLMs for semantic sources are all named topics in the sibling ESWC call. The reviewer pool
   is the one that will actually understand why loading a legally non-copyable third graph beside the other
   two is the point.
3. **The community has said in writing that it wants this shape of paper.** The ESWC 2026 research-track
   call — same community, same reviewers — states that sound approaches that do not outperform the state of
   the art are welcome, and that negative results should be reported. Three of this project's four findings
   are null or negative.
4. **Open review is an asset here, not a cost.** SWJ publishes reviews and reviewer names. A project whose
   distinguishing feature is a version-controlled record where six experiments exist only because earlier
   ones were wrong, and where CI fails the build on any number lacking an experiment ID, benefits from a
   review process that is itself on the record.

Fallbacks, in order: **ECIR 2027 short paper** (6 pages, 2026-10-12) for the grader-calibration finding
alone — that finding needs no external baseline and is a complete paper by itself; **ESWC 2027** if its
call opens on a workable date; **TMLR** if the SWJ audience objection turns out to be wrong-footed.

### 3.2 Tier reachable today, changing nothing

**Workshop.** With no new experiments and no new writing, the honest ceiling is a workshop or a short
paper. The checkable reason: items W1–W13 are all satisfiable from the evidence list as given, whereas
B4 (≥2 runs per number), B9 (external anchor), and B15 (no overclaim) are each currently at *partially* or
*no*, and any one of them is a rejection at B-Tier.

The only workshop with a live deadline is NORA @ AACL-IJCNLP 2026, and I do not recommend it: eight days,
a mismatched theme, and — decisively — it is **archival in the ACL Anthology**, which would consume the
work's unpublished status for a paper that deserves better than a themed workshop it does not fit.

### 3.3 Tier reachable with 4–6 weeks of writing only, no new experiments

**Journal** — specifically SWJ or TMLR, not JAIR.

What four to six weeks of writing buys, concretely:
- J5 and J8: narrow every claim to the arms and the single domain actually measured. This is a writing act,
  and it converts the project's biggest liability (over-broad reading) into a stated scope.
- J7: the grader-calibration study already exists. Writing it up as a first-class section — with the
  explicit statement that two of three local graders cannot resolve a 0.03 gap and one inverts the ordering
  of mediocre versus good answers, and that three close-call results fall inside that resolution limit —
  turns a methodological embarrassment into the paper's most original contribution.
- J6 and J12: disclosing `n_runs: 1`, unrecorded seeds, the two deliberately-unfixed scoring faults with
  their direction, and the six superseded experiments. At conference tiers this is a wound. At journal tier
  it is evidence of a working scientific process.
- J13 and J14: minting a Zenodo DOI for the code, data pointers and record is a day of work, not an
  experiment. This closes A14/B13/J13 outright.

**B-Tier is *not* reliably reachable on writing alone.** I want to be blunt about that. A B-Tier full paper
still fails B4 (several numbers are `n=1`) and B9 (no external anchor at all). A B-Tier *short* paper on the
grader-calibration finding alone is genuinely reachable on writing — call it a coin flip at ECIR 2027 short
— because that finding is self-contained, does not need an external system, and is about the instrument
rather than the system. But the full four-finding paper is not a B-Tier paper today.

### 3.4 Tier requiring new experiments, and which experiments

**A-Tier.** Blocking items A4, A5, A8, A10 and A11 cannot be closed by writing. The specific experiments:

1. **External-system head-to-head (closes A4, A10, A11).** Run at least two *published* systems on the
   identical 288-question held-out set with the identical grading protocol: one published text-to-Cypher or
   text-to-SPARQL system, and one published KG-RAG / KGQA pipeline. Report them in the same table as the
   three arms. Without this, no A-Tier PC will discuss the paper.
2. **Human grading anchor (closes A8).** At least 200 (question, answer) pairs, double-annotated by two or
   more human annotators, with inter-annotator agreement reported, and with each of the two grader families
   correlated against the human labels (Kendall tau or equivalent). Given that the project has *already
   measured* that some graders invert rankings, this is not optional — it is the experiment that decides
   whether any correctness number in the paper means anything.
3. **Seeded replication (closes A5).** Re-run all three arms, both answer positions, both grader families,
   at least three times with recorded seeds. Re-derive all six differences and their bootstrap intervals.
   Pay specific attention to `deterministic − llm_query`, which is currently +0.0822 [+0.0362,+0.1308] under
   family 1 and +0.0643 [−0.0080,+0.1333] under family 2 — three seeded runs will either establish that
   result or kill it, and either outcome is publishable.
4. **Third-party question bank (reinforces A4, and answers the project's own author-bias finding).**
   Evaluate on a question set the project did not author. The project has already measured that
   author-written benchmarks overstate the systems they were written for; continuing to report only on a
   self-authored bank after measuring that effect is the kind of inconsistency reviewers seize on.
5. **Second domain (closes A6).** Port the federation to a second pair of graphs in a different domain with
   different schemas — a biomedical graph plus a bibliographic graph would do — and repeat the three-arm
   comparison. This is the experiment that converts "our system behaves this way" into "schema-derived query
   construction beats templates."
6. **Contamination control.** Probe whether the planning and grading models have memorised ATT&CK and CAPEC
   content, e.g. by substituting synthetic identifiers for real technique IDs and re-measuring. A reviewer
   will ask; there is currently no answer.
7. **Fixed-fault re-measurement.** Fix the two known scoring faults and re-run the headline comparison on a
   frozen snapshot, reporting both the unfixed (comparison-preserving) and fixed numbers side by side. The
   decision to leave them unfixed mid-comparison was correct; leaving them unmeasured is not.

Items 1, 2 and 3 are the minimum for an A-Tier *attempt*. Items 4, 5 and 6 are what make the attempt likely
to succeed.

### 3.5 The strongest reason a reviewer would reject this at A-Tier

**I partly disagree with the project's own assessment.** The absence of an external published baseline is
the reason a reviewer will *write down*, because it is the easiest to state and the hardest to argue with in
a rebuttal. But it is not the deepest problem, and a good A-Tier reviewer will find the deeper one.

The deeper problem is that the paper's entire correctness axis is an LLM grading an LLM, with no human
anchor — and the project has itself produced the evidence that this instrument is unreliable in exactly the
regime the headline experiment operates in. The calibration study found that two of three local graders
cannot express a 0.03 quality difference once answers are already good, and that one of them *inverts* the
ordering of mediocre versus good answers. That is not a caveat; it is a demonstration that the measuring
device is non-monotone in the region where the measurements are being taken. The headline ordering
(`generic` 0.65 > `deterministic` 0.49 > `llm_query` 0.40) involves gaps far larger than 0.03 and would
probably survive, but the `deterministic − llm_query` result — the one that carries the paper's most
quotable claim, that hand-written templates beat a model writing queries — has a family-2 interval of
[−0.0080, +0.1333], i.e. it is *not established* under one of the two graders, on a single run, measured by
an instrument the authors have shown can inject artefacts of comparable size. A reviewer can reject on that
sentence alone, and no rebuttal answers it, because the answer requires a human-labelled subset that does
not exist. Compounding it: one domain, two schemas, `n_runs: 1` on several experiments, seeds unrecorded, no
contamination control, a held-out set that is a random split of a question bank the authors wrote — after
they themselves measured that author-written benchmarks flatter their own systems — and two known scoring
faults deliberately left in, both inflating scores. Individually each is survivable. Together they
constitute "the claims are under-determined by the evidence," which is the standard A-Tier rejection and is,
in this case, correct.

The absence of an external baseline is a *gap*; gaps get "weak reject, address in revision." The
uncharacterised grader is a *validity failure*; validity failures get "reject."

The good news, and it is real: everything in the paragraph above is a reason to publish this at journal tier
rather than a reason not to publish it. Journals — SWJ and TMLR explicitly — accept papers whose claims are
narrowed to the evidence. The grader-calibration finding, which is what makes A-Tier unreachable, is
simultaneously the most novel thing the project has produced. Lead with it.

  - tier: journal
    definition: "No page limit, iterative revision over months, and at TMLR and SWJ specifically an acceptance criterion built on correctness and completeness rather than novelty or significance. The only tier where 'we could not run an external system' is a disclosure rather than a rejection trigger."
    signal: "Published acceptance criteria (TMLR's are explicit and public), open or transparent review (SWJ publishes reviews and reviewer names), and no length constraint."
    requirements:
      - id: J1
        heading: novelty
        text: "Is the claim original and unpublished, with any overlap with prior workshop or conference papers by the same authors declared at submission?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J2
        heading: novelty
        text: "Novelty of method is not required (TMLR: technical correctness over subjective significance; SWJ accepts tool and system reports). Is there at least one reader in the journal's stated audience who would act on this finding, and does the paper name who?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J3
        heading: novelty
        text: "Negative and null results are acceptable at TMLR and SWJ. Is each null result stated as a null - 'we could not detect a difference of size X' - rather than as an absence of effect?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J4
        heading: evidence
        text: "Is every claim in the abstract traceable to a specific experiment identifier reported in the paper or its appendix?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J5
        heading: evidence
        text: "Where evidence does not support the broadest reading of a claim, has the CLAIM been narrowed to match - TMLR's explicit remedy - rather than the evidence overstated?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J6
        heading: evidence
        text: "Are n_runs, seed status and grader identity disclosed per experiment, including for the older experiments where n_runs is 1 and seeds are unrecorded?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J7
        heading: evidence
        text: "Is the grader itself characterised - its failure modes, the smallest quality difference it can resolve, and which of the paper's results fall inside that resolution limit?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J8
        heading: evidence
        text: "Is there a stated scope boundary - one domain, two schemas, two query languages - with no claim generalised past it?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J9
        heading: baselines
        text: "External published baselines are not mandatory at TMLR or SWJ. Is their absence stated, with claims narrowed accordingly (e.g. 'relative to the arms compared here' rather than 'state of the art')?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J10
        heading: baselines
        text: "Is the related work complete enough that a reader can locate the external systems themselves, even though none were run?"
        blocking: true
      - id: J11
        heading: writing
        text: "Is the paper as long as its evidence requires and no longer, rather than exploiting the absence of a page limit (JAIR: 'we strongly encourage authors to be concise')?"
        blocking: false
      - id: J12
        heading: writing
        text: "Does the paper describe the superseded experiments - that six exist only because earlier measurements were wrong, and the wrong versions are retained and marked - since this is a credibility asset at journal review and invisible everywhere else?"
        blocking: false
      - id: J13
        heading: artifact
        text: "Are code, data pointers and the experimental record released under a persistent identifier (DOI), with licence and attribution stated? SWJ and JWS reviewers expect resolvable, permanent resources."
        blocking: true
      - id: J14
        heading: artifact
        text: "Where the journal mandates a reproducibility checklist, is it completed and attached? JAIR desk-rejects submissions without one."
        blocking: true
      - id: J15
        heading: disqualifier
        text: "Is the paper free of the 'merely applies known techniques to an application area without a methodological contribution of general interest' reading, which JAIR lists as a summary-rejection category?"
        blocking: true

recommendation:
  submit_to: "Semantic Web Journal (IOS Press), full research paper, permanent open call - https://www.semantic-web-journal.net/calls"
  reachable_today: "workshop"
  reachable_with_writing_only: "journal"
  requires_new_experiments: "A"
  strongest_rejection_reason: "Not the missing external baseline - that is the reason a reviewer will write down, but it is a gap, and gaps get 'weak reject, address in revision'. The fatal one is that the entire correctness axis is an LLM grading an LLM with no human anchor, in a regime the project has itself shown the instrument to be unreliable in: two of three local graders cannot express a 0.03 quality difference once answers are good, and one inverts the ranking of mediocre versus good answers. The headline ordering (generic 0.65 > deterministic 0.49 > llm_query 0.40) involves gaps large enough to probably survive, but the most quotable claim - templates beat a model writing queries - rests on deterministic - llm_query = +0.0643 [-0.0080, +0.1333] under grader family 2, i.e. not established under one of two graders, on a single run, measured by an instrument capable of injecting artefacts of comparable size. No rebuttal answers that, because the answer requires a human-labelled subset that does not exist. Compounded by one domain, n_runs=1 on several experiments, unrecorded seeds, no contamination control, a held-out split of a self-authored question bank after the project itself measured that author-written benchmarks flatter their own systems, and two known score-inflating faults left unfixed. Together: the claims are under-determined by the evidence. That is a validity failure, not a gap, and validity failures get 'reject'."
